      Times are Mars local solar time, where 12:00 is the sun at its highest. The temperature, wind, humidity and pressure ranges come from the summary of Perseverance's MEDA weather station that was supplied for this project, measured about 1.45 m above the ground. The hour-by-hour curve drawn between those ranges, sunrise at 06:00 and sunset at 18:00, and the 8 °C dust-storm adjustment are estimates.

      Directions

        Suit and crew

        Surface image

        The map surface is a real orbital photograph: the Mars 2020 CTX orthomosaic of Jezero crater, 6 metres per pixel, taken by the Context Camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. It is shown at its full extent, about 30 by 30 km, which is the western half of the crater: the rim, the inlet channel, the delta and the floor out to the middle. It is placed from its own map coordinates, with the landing spot at 18.4447°N 77.4508°E. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS, mosaic by USGS Astrogeology.

        The topographic map layer is the Mars Express HRSC elevation map of Jezero crater, cropped to the same area. Heights are in metres relative to the Mars areoid, with contour lines every 100 m. Credit: © ESA/DLR/FU Berlin, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO.

        You can lay a different image over the terrain, such as a sharper HiRISE crop.

        • USGS HiRISE mosaic of Jezero, 25 cm per pixel, covering 18.31–18.67°N, 77.22–77.58°E
        • NASA: Kodiak and the delta scarps from orbit
        • JPL: Perseverance's ground view of the delta

        How the estimates work

        • Flat-ground pace is 2.7 km/h, the speed Apollo planners assumed for long walks back to the lander (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal). Slopes slow it by Tobler's hiking rule. Sand cuts it to 82% and boulders to 60%.
        • Energy is the walking effort you set, raised 50% on sand and 30% among boulders, plus the work of lifting crew and suit against Mars gravity (3.71 m/s²) at 25% muscle efficiency.
        • Oxygen follows from energy: a body uses about 1 litre of oxygen per 20.1 kJ, so 300 W needs about 77 g an hour.
        • Each Marswalk adds 15 minutes in the airlock at each end and 20 minutes at every stop along the way. A return trip adds 45 minutes of work at the destination; a one-way trip assumes you go inside on arrival instead.
        • The risk score runs from 1 to 100 and is this project’s own scale, not a NASA standard. Oxygen sets most of it: the score is 100 if the tank runs out, 70 to 99 if you finish inside the 30-minute reserve, and falls quickly as the margin grows. Steep ground adds up to 10, sand and boulders up to 5, more than five hours outside up to 15, and weather up to 30 for a dust storm, 25 for darkness and 5 for cold below −60 °C.
        • Radiation uses 0.64 mSv a day, measured by Curiosity in Gale crater (Space.com report).
        • The photograph is real, but the heights under it are not measured. The crater wall, the inlet channel, the delta top, Kodiak, Belva crater and the Séítah sand were traced by eye from the image and given estimated heights on a grid of 100 m cells. The rim and floor heights were set from the contour values on the ESA topographic map, but slopes and climbs are still calculated from this traced model, not read from the map, because the page has no NASA elevation data yet. Place names are positioned approximately. The sand and boulder factors, stop times and default tank size are assumptions you can change or challenge.
